question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
It was difficult to accommodate the avariciousness of the people.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Generosity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Avariciousness" means an excessive desire for wealth or material gain; greed. (लालच, धन-लोलुपता)
◦ Example: His avariciousness made him exploit even his closest friends for money.

• Since the question asks for the ANTONYM, we need a word that means the opposite of greed — that is, willingness to give freely and unselfishly.

• "Generosity" means the quality of being kind and generous, freely giving money, help, or time. (उदारता) This is the direct opposite of greed/avariciousness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Criticism" (आलोचना): The expression of disapproval based on perceived faults; unrelated to greed.

• Option 3: "Hatred" (घृणा): Intense dislike; not the opposite of greed.

• Option 4: "Envy" (ईर्ष्या): A feeling of discontent due to another's possessions; actually closer in meaning to greed, not its opposite.

NOTE

• Related words: avarice, greedy, covetous, miserly (all mean greedy) versus generous, charitable, magnanimous, munificent (all mean the opposite).

• SSC frequently tests antonym pairs built on "greed vs generosity" — remember avarice ↔ generosity, miserly ↔ munificent, stingy ↔ liberal.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
He has written a best-selling novel.
option_1: A best-selling novel was being written by him
option_2: A best-selling novel has been written by him.
option_3: A best-selling novel was written by him.
option_4: A best-selling novel would have been written by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A best-selling novel has been written by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He has written a best-selling novel" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a best-selling novel" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "has" (used with "He") is retained along with "been"; the verb "written" (V3 of write) is kept as is; and "he" becomes "him" after "by".
◦ Passive: A best-selling novel has been written by him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was being written" is the passive form of the Past Continuous Tense, not the Present Perfect.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was written" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "would have been written" changes the tense/mood of the sentence altogether, expressing an unreal past condition, which is not present in the original sentence.

NOTE

• In Present Perfect passive constructions, always use "has/have + been + V3" — never drop the "been", and never confuse it with the Present Perfect Continuous, which cannot normally be converted to passive voice.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P) her face
Q) I have
R) for a year
S) not seen
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. QSPR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A meaningful sentence must begin with the subject "I", so the sentence must start with part Q) "I have".

• After the subject and auxiliary "have", the main verb in its negative form must follow, which is part S) "not seen", giving "I have not seen".

• The verb "seen" requires its object, part P) "her face", giving "I have not seen her face".

• Finally, the time expression, part R) "for a year", completes the sentence: "I have not seen her face for a year."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. QSPR.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PQRS): "Her face I have for a year not seen" — grammatically incorrect and meaningless order.

• Option 2 (PSQR): "Her face not seen I have for a year" — incorrect, breaks the Subject + Auxiliary + Verb structure.

• Option 3 (SPQR): "Not seen her face I have for a year" — incorrect, the negative verb cannot precede the subject.

NOTE

• In Present Perfect sentences, the correct word order is always Subject + have/has + not + V3 + Object + Time expression.

• Always identify the subject first while solving sentence-rearrangement (para jumble) questions — it almost always anchors the first part of the sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word from the following sentence.
Barren

"Can you believe how much traffic there is today?", grumbled Tom, glancing at the congested road ahead.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Congested.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Barren" means land or ground that is bare, empty, and unproductive, incapable of supporting vegetation or life. (बंजर, वीरान, खाली)
◦ Example: The desert stretched out as a barren, lifeless landscape.

• Since the question asks for the ANTONYM, we need a word from the sentence meaning the opposite of "empty/unproductive" — that is, something full, crowded, or overflowing.

• "Congested" means overcrowded or overfull, blocked due to excessive presence of something — the opposite sense of "barren" (empty). (भीडभाड वाला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Believe" (विश्वास करना): To accept something as true; unrelated to barren/fertile.

• Option 2: "Grumbled" (बड़बड़ाना): To complain in a bad-tempered way; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: "Glancing" (सरसरी नजर डालना): To take a quick look; unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "barren": arid, desolate, infertile, sterile.

• Other antonyms of "barren": fertile, fruitful, productive, lush, congested (in the sense of "full/crowded" as opposed to "empty").

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word segment in the given sentence.
A herd of cattle consists of related females, cubs, and a small number of adult males.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. pride of lions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The description "consists of related females, cubs, and a small number of adult males" describes the social structure of lions, which live in a group called a "pride", made up of related lionesses, their cubs, and a few adult males.

• A "herd of cattle" does not fit this description, since cattle herds are not structured this way — this is precisely the standard definition of a lion pride.

• Therefore, the underlined segment must be replaced with the collective noun that correctly matches the description: "pride of lions".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "pack of wolves": A group of wolves is called a pack, typically led by a breeding pair, not matching the given description of a female-and-cub-dominated group.

• Option 3: "school of fish": Refers to a large group of fish swimming together; unrelated to the description given.

• Option 4: "flock of birds": Refers to a group of birds; unrelated to the description given.

NOTE

• Common collective nouns tested by SSC: pride of lions, pack of wolves, herd of cattle/elephants, flock of birds/sheep, school/shoal of fish, troop of monkeys, swarm of bees, pod of whales/dolphins.

• Learn collective nouns along with the typical animal/context they are associated with, as SSC often frames them inside a descriptive sentence like this one rather than asking directly.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the given group of words.
A time when money might unexpectedly be needed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A rainy day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A rainy day" means a possible future time of hardship or financial need, when money might unexpectedly be required, and by extension, "save for a rainy day" means to save money for such an unforeseen need. (मुसीबत का समय)
◦ Example: She always keeps some savings aside for a rainy day.

• This idiom comes from the literal idea that rain can unexpectedly disrupt outdoor plans, so one should always be prepared for unexpected difficulty.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "A raw deal" (अन्यायपूर्ण व्यवहार): Unfair treatment.
◦ Example: He felt he had been given a raw deal by his employer.

• Option 3: "A rash of something" (कई घटनाओं का एक साथ होना): A large number of unwelcome things happening within a short period.

• Option 4: "A rap over the knuckles" (डांट फटकार): A mild punishment or scolding for doing something wrong.

NOTE

• Other money-related idioms often asked in SSC: "to save for a rainy day", "born with a silver spoon in one's mouth" (born rich), "to make ends meet" (to manage with limited money), and "to feather one's nest" (to make oneself wealthy, often dishonestly).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who does not believe in God
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Atheist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Atheist" is a person who does not believe in the existence of God or any deities. (नास्तिक)
◦ Example: As an atheist, he did not participate in any religious rituals.

• This is a standard one-word substitution frequently tested by SSC, built on the prefix "a-" (without) + "theos" (God, from Greek) — literally "without God".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Amateur" (शौकिया): A person who engages in a pursuit as a hobby, not professionally; unrelated meaning.

• Option 2: "Anarchy" (अराजकता): A state of disorder due to absence of authority or government; this is a noun for a condition, not a person.

• Option 3: "Autocrat" (तानाशाह): A ruler who has absolute power, unrelated to religious belief.

NOTE

• Related words: Agnostic (a person who believes nothing can be known about the existence of God, as opposed to an atheist who actively denies it), Theist (a person who believes in God), Pantheist (one who believes God is present in everything).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word..
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Measerement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Measurement" — the act or process of measuring, or the size/amount found by measuring.
◦ Example: The tailor took accurate measurements before stitching the suit.

• Spelling key: MEASURE + MENT. The word "Measerement" wrongly swaps the "u" and "e" in the root word "measure", writing it as "measer" instead of "measur".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Region" — correctly spelt; means an area or division of land.

• Option 3: "Confidential" — correctly spelt; means intended to be kept secret.

• Option 4: "Strengths" — correctly spelt; the plural of "strength", note the "ngth" cluster.

NOTE

• Remember the root "measure" stays intact in all its derived forms: measure, measured, measuring, measurement, measurable.

• Other commonly confused spellings in this pattern: occurrence, maintenance, existence, embarrassment, and questionnaire.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
I saw a shabby looking man living in the cavity of a mountain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. hole.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Cavity" means a hollow space or hole within a solid object, such as a hollow or hole inside a mountain or rock. (गुहा, खोखली जगह/छेद)
◦ Example: Bats often roost in the cavities of caves and old trees.

• In the given sentence, a man is described as living inside the mountain, which means he is living in a hollow space — a "hole" — carved into the mountain, not on any raised or elevated part of it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "elevation" (ऐंग्ल कोण): A raised area or height; the opposite sense of a hollow cavity.

• Option 2: "height" (ऊंचाई): The measurement from base to top; again the opposite of a hollow space.

• Option 3: "mound" (टीला): A raised heap or hill of earth; this too denotes something raised, not hollow.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "cavity" (hollow, hole) with words describing height/elevation such as "summit", "peak", "mound", or "elevation" — these are near-opposite in meaning.

• "Cavity" is also commonly used in the dental sense — a hole in a tooth caused by decay.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A.The door of the flat was ajar.
B.The taxi stopped.
C.Mr. Satterthwaite flung himself out and raced up the stone stairs to the second floor like a young athlete.
D.He pushed it open, and the great voice welcomed him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BCAD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The paragraph must logically begin with the action that starts the sequence of events — the taxi arriving, so it starts with B) "The taxi stopped."

• Once the taxi stops, the natural next action is Mr. Satterthwaite getting out and rushing up the stairs, which is C) "Mr. Satterthwaite flung himself out and raced up the stone stairs to the second floor like a young athlete."

• Having reached the second floor, he would then notice the state of the door, which is A) "The door of the flat was ajar."

• Finally, having found the door ajar, he pushes it open and is welcomed inside, which is D) "He pushed it open, and the great voice welcomed him."

• This gives the logical and chronological sequence: B → C → A → D.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. BCAD.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BACD): Places the observation about the ajar door before the character has even reached the second floor, breaking the logical sequence of events.

• Option 2 (ABCD): Starts with the door being ajar before any character or taxi has even been introduced, which makes no coherent sense.

• Option 4 (DCBA): Reverses the entire sequence, having the door pushed open before the taxi has even stopped, which is chronologically impossible.

NOTE

• In paragraph (sentence) rearrangement questions, look for the sentence that introduces the setting/action first (often involving arrival, such as a vehicle stopping) — it usually opens the paragraph, while cause must always precede effect.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
He wrote an inspiring speech for the event.
option_1: An inspiring speech was being written by him for the event.
option_2: An inspiring speech was written by him for the event.
option_3: An inspiring speech is written by him for the event.
option_4: An inspiring speech has been written by him for the event.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. An inspiring speech was written by him for the event.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He wrote an inspiring speech for the event" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "an inspiring speech" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "wrote" becomes its past participle "written"; and "he" becomes "him" with "by".
◦ Passive: An inspiring speech was written by him for the event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was being written" is the passive of the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is written" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "has been written" is the passive of the Present Perfect Tense.

NOTE

• Always identify the tense of the active sentence first before converting to passive — the auxiliary verb used in the passive must always match the tense of the original active sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
It is nothing else your pride which makes you say such a thing.
option_3: else but your pride which make
option_4: else but your pride which makes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. else but your pride which makes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The word "else" is idiomatically followed by "but" in constructions like "nothing else but...", meaning "nothing other than". Simply saying "nothing else your pride" is grammatically incomplete and non-idiomatic; "but" must be inserted after "else".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: The relative pronoun "which" here refers back to the singular subject "your pride", so it must take the singular verb "makes", not the plural "make".

• Applying both rules together: "It is nothing else but your pride which makes you say such a thing."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "else your pride that makes" is incorrect because it omits the necessary word "but" after "else".

• Option 2: "else your pride which make" is incorrect for the same reason (missing "but"), and additionally uses the plural verb "make" with the singular subject "pride".

• Option 3: "else but your pride which make" correctly inserts "but" but wrongly uses the plural verb "make" instead of "makes".

NOTE

• Common idiomatic pairs tested by SSC: "nothing else but", "no sooner...than", "scarcely...when", "not only...but also" — learn these fixed combinations, as SSC frequently tests missing linking words within them.

• Always check subject-verb agreement separately from idiom/preposition errors, as questions often combine both types of errors in one sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
This is a clear example of conflict of egos.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. clash.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Conflict" means a serious disagreement or clash, typically a prolonged struggle between opposing forces, ideas, or interests. (टकराव, संघर्ष)
◦ Example: There was a conflict of interest between the two business partners.

• "Clash" means a strong disagreement or a violent confrontation between opposing people or forces, which closely matches the meaning of "conflict" in this context. (टकराव)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "mingling" (मिलना-जुलना): To mix or mix socially with others; the opposite sense of conflict, which implies harmony rather than opposition.

• Option 3: "infliction" (आघात पहुंचाना): The act of forcing something unpleasant, such as pain or punishment, on someone; not a synonym for disagreement between two parties.

• Option 4: "crash" (टकराना, दुर्घटना): Usually refers to a physical collision or a sudden failure (e.g., of a system or market), not an abstract disagreement of egos.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "conflict": strife, discord, friction, feud, confrontation.

• Antonyms of "conflict": harmony, agreement, concord, accord.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Mr. Adhil called back but he wasn’t able to find the scooter part he needed.
option_1: called down but he wasn’t able to
option_2: called off but he wasn’t able to
option_3: called around but he wasn’t able to
option_4: called up to but he wasn’t able to
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. called around but he wasn't able to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "call around" means to telephone or visit several different people or places one after another, typically to find or ask about something. (कई जगह/लोगों से संपर्क करना)
◦ Example: She called around to different shops to find the spare part.

• In the given context, Mr. Adhil is trying to locate a specific scooter part, which logically requires contacting multiple shops or people — this is exactly the meaning conveyed by "called around", making it the most sensible substitute.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "called down" means to reprimand or scold someone, which does not fit the context of searching for a spare part.

• Option 2: "called off" means to cancel something, which is unrelated to the act of searching for a part.

• Option 4: "called up to" is not a standard, meaningful phrasal verb combination in English.

NOTE

• Common phrasal verbs with "call": call off (cancel), call on (visit someone/request someone to speak), call for (require/demand), call up (telephone someone/summon for military service), call around (contact several places), call back (return a phone call).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
Instead of confusing others, let us call a spade a spade in front of the audience.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Speak truthfully.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To call a spade a spade" means to speak frankly and directly about something, describing it exactly as it is, without avoiding unpleasant facts. (स्पष्ट व सच बात कहना)
◦ Example: He always calls a spade a spade, even if the truth is uncomfortable.

• The idiom originates from ancient Greek, meaning that a simple tool (a spade) should be called by its plain, correct name rather than something more polite or roundabout.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Pretend superiority": Unrelated meaning; this describes arrogance, not honesty.

• Option 2: "Remain silent": The opposite of the idiom's meaning, which is about speaking out plainly.

• Option 4: "Be at strife": Means to be in conflict, which is not the meaning of this idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms about honesty/directness often tested by SSC: "straight from the horse's mouth" (direct/reliable information), "in black and white" (in writing), "to speak one's mind" (to say exactly what one thinks).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Neccessary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Necessary" — needed to be done, essential or required.
◦ Example: It is necessary to submit the form before the deadline.

• Spelling key: remember it has one "C" and two "S"s — Ne-c-e-ss-ary. The incorrect form "Neccessary" wrongly doubles the "c" and uses a single "s".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Connoisseur" — correctly spelt; a person with expert knowledge in a particular field, especially the arts.

• Option 3: "Privilege" — correctly spelt; a special right or advantage.

• Option 4: "Dilemma" — correctly spelt; a situation requiring a choice between equally undesirable options.

NOTE

• Memory trick for "necessary": one Collar (C), two Socks (SS).

• Other commonly confused spellings with double/single letters: occurrence, embarrass, accommodate, harass, recommend.

question:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.
We need to __________ a solution to this problem before it gets worse.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. come up with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "come up with" means to think of or produce an idea, plan, or solution. (सुझाव/समाधान देना/निकालना)
◦ Example: The team came up with a brilliant solution to the crisis.

• In the given sentence, the context requires finding/producing a solution to a worsening problem, which is exactly the sense conveyed by "come up with".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "cut down on" means to reduce the amount of something (e.g., cut down on sugar); does not fit the context of producing a solution.

• Option 2: "break down" means to stop functioning, or to divide into smaller parts, or to become upset; does not fit here.

• Option 3: "break up" means to end a relationship or to separate into pieces; does not fit here.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs meaning "to think of/produce an idea": think up, hit upon, work out.

• Common phrasal verbs with "break": break down, break up, break out (start suddenly, as in a fire/war), break away (escape/separate).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined word in the given sentence.
This building is colossal and it can hold a village’s population in it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. very huge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Colossal" means extremely large in size, extent, or degree; huge or gigantic. (विशाल, बहुत बड़ा)
◦ Example: The colossal statue could be seen from miles away.

• The sentence itself supports this meaning, since a building large enough to hold an entire village's population must be extremely huge in size.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "temporary" (अस्थायी): Lasting for a limited time; unrelated to size.

• Option 3: "very beautiful" (बहुत सुंदर): Relates to appearance, not size.

• Option 4: "puny" (तुच्छ, छोटा): Means small and weak — the direct opposite of "colossal".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "colossal": gigantic, immense, massive, enormous, mammoth, vast.

• Antonyms of "colossal": puny, tiny, minute, diminutive.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Maverick
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Bohemian.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Maverick" means an unorthodox or independent-minded person who does not conform to accepted rules, ideas, or behaviour of a group. (स्वतंत्र विचारों वाला व्यक्ति, अपरंपरागत व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: He was seen as a maverick in the industry for rejecting traditional business practices.

• "Bohemian" means a socially unconventional person, often associated with an artistic or alternative lifestyle, which closely matches the sense of "maverick" as someone who breaks away from conventional norms. (परंपरा से हटकर जीवन जीने वाला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Conformist" (परंपरावादी): A person who conforms to accepted behaviour or beliefs — the opposite of a maverick.

• Option 2: "Orthodox" (रूढ़िवादी): Following traditional or established beliefs and practices — again opposite in meaning.

• Option 4: "Follower" (अनुयायी): A person who follows another's lead or beliefs — opposite of the independent-mindedness implied by "maverick".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "maverick": nonconformist, rebel, dissenter, individualist.

• SSC frequently frames such questions with 2-3 antonym-like distractors alongside the correct synonym — always eliminate options with clearly opposite meaning first.

question:
Identify the error in the given sentence.
Camels tend to move slowly than other domestic animals in the plains.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. move slowly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Comparative Degree: Whenever the word "than" is used in a sentence to compare two things, the adjective/adverb before it must be in the comparative degree, usually formed by adding "-er" or using "more" before the word.

• Since the sentence uses "than other domestic animals", the adverb "slowly" before it must also be in the comparative form, i.e., "more slowly", not the plain/positive form "slowly".

• Corrected sentence: "Camels tend to move more slowly than other domestic animals in the plains."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "domestic animals in the plains." — this part is grammatically correct as it stands.

• Option 2: "than other" — this is correctly used, as "than" is the appropriate comparative conjunction here.

• Option 4: "Camels tend to" — this part is grammatically correct; "tend to" is a correctly used verb phrase.

NOTE

• Whenever "than" appears in a sentence, always check that the preceding adjective/adverb is in the comparative form (e.g., "more slowly", "faster", "better", "taller") — this is one of the most frequently tested error types in SSC exams.

• Common comparative errors tested: using positive degree with "than", using "more" with words that already have "-er" (double comparatives, e.g. "more better" is wrong).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.

The mathematician Federico Ardila-Mantilla grew up in Colombia, an (1)_______________ student but gifted in math. He was failing most of his classes at his high school in Bogotá when someone (2)_________________ him to apply to MIT. He had not heard of the school. To his surprise, he got in, and he went on scholarship. Mathematically, he did well. One of his professors, an acid-tongued theoretician known to (3)_____________ his audience to a herd of cows, routinely tucked ‘open’ math problems into homework assignments, without telling the students. These had never been solved by anyone. Ardila solved one. He went on to receive his bachelor’s and Ph.D. in math from MIT.
But his academic experience was also one of isolation. Part of it had to do with his own (4)_______________. Part of it was cultural. As a Latino, he was very much in the minority in the department, and he did not feel comfortable in American mathematical spaces. No one had tried to explicitly (5)_________________ him, yet he felt alone. In math, collaborating with others opens up new kinds of learning and thinking. But in his nine years at MIT, Ardila worked with others only twice.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. indifferent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes Federico Ardila-Mantilla's attitude towards his studies as a student, and the passage explicitly states that "he was failing most of his classes at his high school", despite being "gifted in math".

• The word "indifferent" here means lacking interest or enthusiasm; showing no particular concern, which logically explains why a mathematically gifted student would still be failing most of his classes — he simply was not an engaged or attentive student overall.

• The sentence structure "an indifferent student but gifted in math" uses "but" to set up a contrast, which fits perfectly with someone who does not apply himself generally, yet still excels specifically in mathematics.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "apprehensive" means fearful or anxious about something; this does not logically explain why he was failing most of his classes.

• Option 2: "apologetic" means feeling or expressing regret; this does not fit the description of a student's academic performance.

• Option 4: "excellent" contradicts the passage directly, since it states he was "failing most of his classes" — an excellent student would not be failing.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check the surrounding contrast words like "but", "yet", or "however" — they usually signal that the blank must contain a word that creates a logical contrast with the following/preceding clause.

• Here, "indifferent...but gifted in math" is a contrast between his general attitude and his specific talent.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. suggested.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage states that despite failing most of his classes, someone encouraged/recommended that Ardila apply to MIT, a fact that surprised him since "he had not heard of the school" before.

• The word "suggested" means to put forward an idea or plan for consideration; to recommend, which fits the context of someone recommending that he apply to a school he had never even heard of.

• The following sentence, "To his surprise, he got in", further confirms that someone had positively recommended/suggested he try, and it worked out unexpectedly well.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "dissuaded" means to persuade someone not to do something — this is the opposite of what is needed, since he did end up applying and getting in.

• Option 3: "removed" does not make sense grammatically or logically in this context — one cannot "remove" a person "to apply to" a school.

• Option 4: "dispirited" means to make someone lose enthusiasm or hope — this does not fit the structure "someone ______ him to apply to MIT", which requires a verb meaning to encourage/recommend.

NOTE

• "Suggest/recommend someone to do something" and "dissuade someone from doing something" are commonly contrasted in cloze passages — always check whether the surrounding context implies encouragement or discouragement.

• Words with similar meaning to "suggested" in this context: recommended, urged, encouraged, prompted.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. compare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes what the acid-tongued (sharp-tongued/sarcastic) professor was known for doing — namely, likening his students/audience to something else, specifically "a herd of cows".

• The word "compare" means to liken one thing to another, pointing out similarities, which fits perfectly with the structure "known to compare his audience to a herd of cows" — a sarcastic professor mocking his students by comparing them to cattle.

• This matches the description of the professor as "acid-tongued", meaning sharp and biting in speech, consistent with making an insulting comparison of his students to cows.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "malign" means to speak ill of someone falsely, but it does not fit the specific structure "known to ______ his audience to a herd of cows", which requires a verb of comparison, not defamation.

• Option 4: "differentiate" means to recognize or establish a difference between things, which is the opposite of what is needed — the professor is drawing a similarity (comparison) between his audience and cows, not a difference.

NOTE

• The phrase "compare X to Y" is a standard fixed collocation meaning to liken X to Y, often used ironically or sarcastically, as in this passage.

• Don't confuse "compare to" (highlighting similarity) with "compare with" (used more for detailed comparison of similarities/differences), and "contrast with" (highlighting difference).

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. introversion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage explains that Ardila's academic isolation had two causes: one personal/psychological, and one cultural (being a Latino minority in the department).

• The word "introversion" means the state of being predominantly concerned with one's own thoughts rather than with external things or other people; a reserved, inward-looking personality, which fits the phrase **"Part of it had to do with his own ______"**, referring to a personal trait that contributed to his sense of isolation.

• This matches the contrast set up in the passage: "Part of it had to do with his own introversion. Part of it was cultural." — one personal cause, one social/cultural cause.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "molestation" refers to harassment or abuse, which is not supported anywhere in the passage and does not fit the context of academic isolation due to personality.

• Option 4: "interrogation" means formal or systematic questioning; this does not fit the context of a personal trait causing isolation.

• "Introversion" (inward-focused personality) is the opposite of "extroversion" (outward-focused, sociable personality) — a commonly tested word pair in vocabulary-based cloze passages.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. exclude.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states: **"No one had tried to explicitly ______ him, yet he felt alone." The word "yet"** signals a contrast — even though no one openly/deliberately did the stated action to him, he still felt alone.

• The word "exclude" means to deliberately leave someone out of a group or activity; to shut someone out, which fits the sentence perfectly: nobody had openly/explicitly excluded him from the department, yet, despite this, he still felt isolated and alone due to being in the minority.

• This matches the overall theme of the paragraph — his isolation was not caused by deliberate, open exclusion by others, but rather stemmed from subtler cultural discomfort of being a minority in the department.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "fabricate" means to invent or make up something falsely; this does not logically fit with "yet he felt alone", as fabricating something about him would not directly relate to feeling excluded/alone.

• Option 3: "incorporate" means to include as part of a whole; this is the opposite of what is needed, and using it would create an illogical sentence ("no one had tried to explicitly include him, yet he felt alone" reverses the intended contrast about isolation).

• Option 4: "stratify" means to arrange into different layers, groups, or classes; it does not fit the personal, direct context of the sentence.

NOTE

• "Exclude" and "include"/"incorporate" are direct antonyms — always check whether the sentence's contrast word (like "yet", "but", "however") requires a positive or negative sense of inclusion.

• Related words: ostracize (to exclude someone from a group deliberately), alienate (to make someone feel isolated), marginalize (to treat someone as insignificant, pushing them to the periphery).
